Compute length-scale bounds for a squared-exponential GP

Source: R/model-prep.R
gp_lengthscale_bounds.Rd

Computes lower and upper bounds for the length-scale \(\ell\) of a squared-exponential (exponentiated-quadratic) kernel, \(k(h) = \exp(-h^2 / (2\ell^2))\), from the spread of the pairwise distances between the points. fit_bayesian_spatial_model() calibrates its length-scale prior over them. The effective range, where the correlation drops to 5 percent, is \(\ell \sqrt{2 \ln 20} \approx 2.45\,\ell\).

Usage

gp_lengthscale_bounds(coords_xy, q_small = 0.25, max_n = 1000L)

Arguments

coords_xy

Numeric matrix or data.frame of coordinates with at least two columns; the first two are used, and replicated rows are collapsed before the distance quantiles are taken, because brms::gp() (gr = TRUE, its default) reduces its covariates to unique rows: a station sampled many times would otherwise weight the quantile by how often it was measured rather than by where the sites are. A row with a coordinate that is missing, not finite or beyond 1e150 has no location: it is left out, with a warning of class spatialkit_rows_dropped that gives the count.

q_small

Quantile of the pairwise distances for the lower bound, a single number in [0, 1]. Default 0.25. On clustered data a low quantile reflects the spacing within clusters.

max_n

Maximum number of distinct points to use in the distance computation. Default 1000. Set to Inf to use all of them. Above it, a subsample is drawn with a fixed seed from the distinct points in coordinate order, so the bounds do not depend on the row order of coords_xy, and the caller's random-number stream is left where it was.

Value

Named numeric vector c(lower, upper): length-scales in the units of coords_xy. lower is the q_small quantile of the distinct pairwise distances divided by \(\sqrt{2 \ln 20}\) (about 2.45); upper is the largest pairwise distance divided by the same factor, and at least 1.2 times lower. c(lower = 0.001, upper = 1) when fewer than two distinct located rows or no positive distances remain. fit_bayesian_spatial_model() standardises the coordinates before it calls this function, so its bounds are in those standardised units.

Details

The lower bound is the q_small quantile of the pairwise distances (by default the 25th percentile) taken as an effective range, and the upper bound is the largest pairwise distance taken as an effective range. The inverse-gamma prior that fit_bayesian_spatial_model() calibrates on them puts 1 percent of its mass below the lower bound and 1 percent above the upper. Both are fixed fractions of the spread of pairwise distances, so they do not shrink as points are added to the same area: more points help the data identify a short range, but they make neither these bounds nor the basis derived from them finer.

These are the bounds a length-scale prior is calibrated over, not the scales a fitted model can resolve, which depend on the basis size (gp_k in fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), which reports it as $info$gp_ell_min, and in CRS units as $info$gp_resolution). A surface whose range is shorter than the lower bound needs a basis fine enough to represent it and a prior that allows it. A larger gp_k under the prior calibrated here changes almost nothing, because the prior still holds the length-scale above this bound. fit_bayesian_spatial_model() therefore moves the prior's lower tail down to the length-scale the basis resolves whenever gp_resolution or an explicit gp_k asks for a finer basis than the one derived from these bounds.

Large layers are subsampled (max_n) to bound the cost of the pairwise distances, which grows with the square of the points.

See also

Other model fitting: fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), fit_gwr_model(), fit_rf_model(), new_spatial_fit()

Examples

# 500 points spread evenly over a square of side 100 km, in metres.
set.seed(1)
xy <- cbind(runif(500, 0, 1e5), runif(500, 0, 1e5))
b <- gp_lengthscale_bounds(xy)
b
#>    lower    upper 
#> 13445.22 55051.07 
# The bounds as effective ranges: the 25th percentile of the pairwise
# distances, about a third of the side, and the largest distance.
b * sqrt(2 * log(20))
#>     lower     upper 
#>  32910.48 134751.08
